subject: Mixed
description: Hard-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy, General Surgery & Orthopedics, Kinesio Therapeutics, Medicine, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Pharmacology, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiology, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences, Psychiatry.

questions.question: A 'Bankart lesion' of the shoulder refers to:

options.A: Detachment of the anteroinferior labrum, commonly occurring with traumatic anterior dislocation
options.B: A tear confined strictly to the superior labrum (10 to 2 o'clock position)
options.C: A rotator cuff tear with no labral involvement
options.D: A fracture of the greater tuberosity

questions.explanation: A Bankart lesion is a tear of the anteroinferior labrum (roughly the 3 to 7 o'clock position in the right shoulder), most commonly occurring with a traumatic anterior dislocation, also compromising the stability of the inferior glenohumeral ligament.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Tests for Labral Tears
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: When testing hip abductor strength in a patient with an unstable knee, resistance is applied at the distal femur (just above the knee) instead of at the ankle. Using this shorter lever, what is the highest grade that can be assigned, even if the patient tolerates maximal resistance?

options.A: Grade 5
options.B: Grade 4
options.C: Grade 3
options.D: Grade 2

questions.explanation: A shorter lever (resistance near the knee rather than at the ankle) makes the test mechanically easier, so a patient who takes maximal resistance in this position can still only be graded a 4 — the longer lever at the ankle is needed to truly demonstrate Grade 5 strength, since it better reflects the functional demand of gait.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Although bulimic episodes (binge eating followed by vomiting) can occur in BOTH anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, the key distinguishing feature is that patients with bulimia nervosa:

options.A: Usually maintain a near-normal body weight (or are overweight), unlike the marked underweight seen in anorexia nervosa
options.B: Always have amenorrhoea, unlike anorexia nervosa patients
options.C: Never show any body-image disturbance
options.D: Are exclusively male, while anorexia nervosa is exclusively female

questions.explanation: While bulimic episodes are common in anorexia nervosa, patients with bulimia nervosa usually maintain a near-normal body weight or are even overweight — sharply contrasting with the significant, often severe underweight state that defines anorexia nervosa.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Eating Disorders — Anorexia Nervosa, Differential Diagnosis
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: A hamartoma is best defined as:

options.A: A malignant tumour of embryonal blastema seen mainly in infants
options.B: A benign tumour composed of mature but disorganised cells/tissues that are normally indigenous to that organ
options.C: An ectopic island of otherwise completely normal tissue in the wrong location
options.D: A tumour combining epithelial and mesenchymal malignant elements

questions.explanation: A hamartoma is a benign lesion made up of mature, differentiated tissue elements that are normal to the organ in question, just disorganised/jumbled — e.g. a pulmonary hamartoma contains mature cartilage, smooth muscle, and epithelium, all normal bronchial components arranged abnormally. This is distinct from a choristoma (ectopic normal tissue in the wrong site) and from blastomas (embryonal tumours of children).
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: 'Idiosyncrasy' as an adverse drug reaction is best defined as:

options.A: A predictable, dose-related toxic effect seen in all patients given a high enough dose
options.B: A genetically determined, abnormal reactivity to a drug, restricted to individuals with a particular (often unique) genetic makeup
options.C: An immunologically mediated reaction requiring prior sensitization
options.D: The normal, expected therapeutic effect of the drug

questions.explanation: Idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a drug — the drug interacts with some unique feature of the individual not found in most people, producing an uncharacteristic reaction restricted to individuals with a particular genotype (e.g. chloramphenicol producing aplastic anaemia in rare individuals).
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: In the tibial external rotation (Dial) test, if the tibia rotates MORE at 90° of knee flexion than at 30°, this pattern most likely indicates injury to:

options.A: Only the popliteus corner (isolated posterolateral injury)
options.B: Both the popliteus corner AND the posterior cruciate ligament
options.C: The anterior cruciate ligament in isolation
options.D: The medial meniscus only

questions.explanation: In the Dial test, if the tibia rotates less at 90° than at 30°, an isolated posterolateral (popliteus corner) injury is more likely. If it rotates MORE at 90° than at 30°, combined injury to both the popliteus corner and the posterior cruciate ligament is more likely.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tibial External Rotation (Dial) Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: For a RISING (increasing) current applied over a superficial nerve, which electrode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse, and why is the active electrode typically connected to it?

options.A: The anode, because it requires less current overall
options.B: The cathode, because it produces contraction of innervated muscle with less current than is required at the anode
options.C: Neither electrode has any different effect
options.D: The anode always requires less current than the cathode

questions.explanation: For a rising current, the cathode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse than the anode. This is why the active electrode is conventionally connected to the cathode — it produces contraction of innervated muscle using less current than would be needed if the anode were used as the active electrode.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: The acute inflammatory stage of soft tissue healing typically lasts approximately how long, unless the insult is perpetuated?

options.A: 4 to 6 days
options.B: 6 months to 1 year
options.C: 2 to 3 years
options.D: Only a few minutes

questions.explanation: The acute inflammatory stage typically lasts 4 to 6 days unless the injury is continually aggravated. The subsequent subacute (proliferation/repair) stage usually lasts 10-17 days (up to 6 weeks in poorly vascularised tissues like tendons), and the chronic (maturation/remodeling) stage can last 6 months to 1 year.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Acute Stage
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: A drug that reacts with an enzyme's catalytic site so strongly (via a covalent bond or very high affinity) that the normal substrate cannot displace it produces which kinetic pattern?

options.A: kM unchanged, Vmax unchanged (no real inhibition)
options.B: kM decreased, Vmax increased
options.C: kM increased and Vmax reduced — a non-equilibrium type of competitive inhibition
options.D: Only Vmax changes while kM decreases proportionally

questions.explanation: Classical competitive inhibition (equilibrium type) raises kM but leaves Vmax unchanged, since enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor. But when the inhibitor binds essentially irreversibly at the same catalytic site (e.g. organophosphates on cholinesterase, or methotrexate's very high affinity for dihydrofolate reductase), substrate can no longer displace it — this non-equilibrium type raises kM AND reduces Vmax.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: The hallmark polysomnographic finding in narcolepsy is:

options.A: Increased REM latency (REM sleep delayed beyond 100 minutes)
options.B: Decreased REM latency, with REM sleep occurring within about 10 minutes of sleep onset
options.C: Complete absence of REM sleep
options.D: No measurable difference from normal sleep architecture

questions.explanation: The hallmark of narcolepsy is decreased REM latency — normal REM latency is 90-100 minutes, but in narcolepsy REM sleep typically begins within about 10 minutes of sleep onset.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Using the KT-1000 arthrometer, a difference of more than 3 mm in anterior displacement between the injured and uninjured knee is generally considered:

options.A: A normal finding requiring no further action
options.B: Diagnostic for injury to the anterior or posterior cruciate ligament
options.C: Evidence of a meniscal tear specifically, never a ligament injury
options.D: Only relevant in paediatric patients

questions.explanation: A side-to-side difference of more than 3 mm in anterior displacement on KT-1000 arthrometer testing is generally considered diagnostic for injury to the anterior cruciate ligament or posterior cruciate ligament.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: The final descent of the testis into the scrotum during fetal development is mediated primarily by:

options.A: Oestrogen from the placenta
options.B: Testosterone from the fetal testis
options.C: Growth hormone from the fetal pituitary
options.D: Prolactin from the maternal circulation

questions.explanation: While gonadal induction (forming a testis in the first place) is driven by genes on the Y chromosome and initial abdominal migration is guided by the gubernaculum, the final descent of the testis into the scrotum is mediated by testosterone produced by the fetal testis itself.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Genital Development
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: What is the minimum daily urine output generally required to adequately excrete the end products of protein metabolism?

options.A: 50 mL/day
options.B: 400 mL/day
options.C: 5000 mL/day
options.D: There is no minimum requirement

questions.explanation: A minimum urine output of approximately 400 mL/day is required to excrete the nitrogenous end products of protein metabolism, even though average daily urine output in a healthy adult is around 1500 mL/day.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: In the 'ischemic penumbra' surrounding the core of an acute ischemic stroke, neurons:

options.A: Die immediately within seconds, identical to the ischemic core
options.B: Survive for a somewhat longer period than core neurons, but will die without timely reperfusion — making this tissue a key target for acute treatment
options.C: Are completely unaffected by the stroke
options.D: Regenerate spontaneously without any intervention

questions.explanation: While neurons in the ischemic core die within minutes, the surrounding penumbra contains neurons that survive somewhat longer but remain at risk — cell survival depends on the severity and duration of ischemia, and without timely reperfusion, cells in the penumbra will die and the infarct will expand. This makes the penumbra the key target of emergency stroke treatment.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Cerebral edema following ischemic stroke typically reaches its maximum at approximately what time point, and is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke?

options.A: Within the first hour
options.B: 3 to 4 days
options.C: 6 months
options.D: It never resolves

questions.explanation: Cerebral edema begins within minutes of the ischemic insult and reaches its maximum by 3 to 4 days, gradually subsiding by 2 to 3 weeks. Significant edema, particularly with large MCA/ICA infarcts, is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke due to raised intracranial pressure and brainstem herniation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The Na+-K+ pump is described as 'electrogenic at rest' because it operates with a coupling ratio of 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in. What would happen to its contribution to the membrane potential if the coupling ratio were instead 1:1?

options.A: It would generate an even larger membrane potential
options.B: It would not directly generate any membrane potential itself, though it would still maintain the concentration gradients the potential depends on
options.C: The cell would immediately depolarise completely and stay depolarised
options.D: The pump would stop functioning altogether

questions.explanation: At a 3:2 coupling ratio, the Na+-K+ pump moves net positive charge out of the cell with each cycle, directly contributing a small electrogenic component to the membrane potential. If the ratio were 1:1 (equal charge moved each way), the pump itself would not generate any net potential directly — though it would still be essential for maintaining the ionic concentration gradients that the resting membrane potential fundamentally depends on.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Genesis of Resting Membrane Potential
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Persistence of red-coloured lochia well beyond the normal expected duration most likely signifies:

options.A: Normal healing with no clinical concern
options.B: Subinvolution of the uterus or retained bits of the conceptus
options.C: A completely normal variant seen in all women
options.D: Onset of the first postpartum menstrual period

questions.explanation: Persistence of the red colour of lochia beyond the normal limit is a clinically important sign suggesting subinvolution of the uterus or retained products of conception, and should prompt further evaluation.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Under conditions of fatigue or cognitive overload, the brain tends to:

options.A: Shift towards more careful, deliberate Type 2 thinking
options.B: Revert to Type 1 (fast, intuitive) processing to conserve cognitive energy, increasing the risk of bias-driven error
options.C: Stop making decisions altogether
options.D: Show no measurable change in decision-making style

questions.explanation: The brain regions required for effortful Type 2 processing are most affected by fatigue and cognitive overload; under these conditions the brain reverts to faster, less effortful Type 1 processing to conserve energy — which is exactly when cognitive biases are more likely to lead to error.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Clot retraction, which produces a more effective and compact haemostatic plug, is driven by contraction of platelet pseudopodia containing which contractile protein?

options.A: Thrombosthenin (actomyosin-like protein)
options.B: Myoglobin
options.C: Collagen
options.D: Fibrinogen exclusively

questions.explanation: Clot retraction (the fibrin clot contracting to about 40% of its original volume within 5-30 minutes) is produced by contraction of platelet pseudopodia, which contain the contractile actomyosin-like protein historically called thrombosthenin.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Isolated haemoptysis (coughing up blood), even when the chest radiograph appears normal, may be the first sign of which condition?

options.A: Bronchogenic carcinoma
options.B: Simple viral upper respiratory tract infection
options.C: Asthma exclusively
options.D: Hyperventilation syndrome

questions.explanation: Isolated haemoptysis can be the first sign of bronchogenic carcinoma even when the chest X-ray is normal, which is why it should always be taken seriously and investigated further rather than dismissed.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition
